description: Unique identifier of the transaction.
pitfall: Looks sequential and correlates with time; it is an identifier, never a feature.

description: Merchant that received the payment.
pitfall: 70.7% of merchants appear once. Any per-merchant rate needs a minimum volume filter.

description: Cardholder placing the transaction.
pitfall: Behaves like a merchant-side customer id (only 0.9% of users appear at more than one merchant) and is created by the customer at sign-up, so it is attacker-controlled.

description: Masked card number: first 6 digits (BIN) plus last 4.
pitfall: Pseudo-identifier only — two different cards from the same issuer can collide on the last 4 digits.

description: Date and time of the transaction, microsecond precision.
pitfall: No timezone declared; a single timezone is assumed. Sort by this before any time-based feature.

description: Transaction amount.
pitfall: No currency declared (BRL assumed). Strongly right-skewed — use the median, not the mean, to describe it.

description: Identifier of the device used in the transaction.
pitfall: 26% missing. Absence is a category, not dirt — dropping those rows removes a quarter of the base. In this sample each device belongs to a single user.

description: Whether the transaction received a fraud-related chargeback. The fraud label.
pitfall: Never use as an input feature. It is a LAGGING label: the dispute arrives days to weeks after the transaction, so recent fraud is still marked FALSE.

description: Hour of day of the transaction.
pitfall: Describes when the attacker operates, not why. Low-volume hours produce meaningless rates — filter by minimum volume before ranking.

description: Whether a device identifier was captured.
pitfall: In this base, missing device has a LOWER chargeback rate (8.1% vs 13.7%) — the intuitive rule would have been wrong.

description: Bank Identification Number: first 6 digits of the card, identifying the issuer.
pitfall: Keep it as text — parsing to integer destroys leading zeros.

description: Last four digits of the card.
pitfall: Only meaningful combined with the BIN.

description: Number of transactions by this user across the entire dataset.
pitfall: Counts transactions that happen AFTER the current one. Descriptive only — the real-time equivalent is a rolling window of prior transactions.

description: Distinct cards used by this user across the entire dataset.
pitfall: Same future leakage; the operational version counts only cards seen before now.

description: Distinct users that used this card across the entire dataset.
pitfall: Same future leakage. Also inherits the masked-card collision caveat.

description: Distinct users that used this device across the entire dataset.
pitfall: Always 1 in this sample — the device-sharing hypothesis could not be tested here.

description: Number of transactions of this merchant across the entire dataset.
pitfall: Future leakage; use as a volume filter for descriptive rankings only.

description: Seconds elapsed since the previous transaction of the same user.
pitfall: Null on a user's first transaction — treat null as 'no history', not as zero.

description: Seconds elapsed since the previous transaction on the same card.
pitfall: Same null caveat as the user version.

description: Amount of the previous transaction on the same card.
pitfall: Used for the card-testing pattern (small probe followed by a large charge); without declined authorizations in the data this pattern is nearly invisible.

description: Transaction amount divided by the median amount of the same user.
pitfall: The median includes future transactions, and with 1.18 transactions per user most users have a median equal to the transaction itself, giving a ratio of 1.0.

description: Number of chargebacks this user had strictly before the current transaction.
pitfall: Correct in ordering (no future rows), but NOT knowable in real time: 82.6% of these transactions occur within 24h of the disputed one, weeks before the dispute exists. Belongs in a block list, never in an authorization rule.

description: Whether the user already had at least one chargeback before this transaction.
pitfall: 89.8% of these transactions are fraud, which makes it the most tempting and least usable signal in the dataset. See the dispute-delay table in the report.
